speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, that was on procedure, but if it was impossible to agree on procedure at the outset, I fail to see where there is much likelihood of agreement upon the actual questions which might be submitted for consideration. However, I mention these things not at all to disguise the importance of the question. I agree entirely with the right hon. leader of the opposition that we must find a way, or make it, to have the question of the revision of our constitution somehow considered. The constitutional relations of the dominions and the United Kingdom presented in itself a very large problem, the question whether or not in the course of time a new status had not been reached by the dominions. That question seemed the most difficult which it was possible for the British government and the governments of the dominions to face, but they were able to discuss these matters at imperial conferences, and out of their discussions was evolved a British statute which we have been quoting recently in this house, the Statute of Westminster, which to all intents and purposes, makes clear the relative powers of the dominion parliaments and of the parliament at Westminster, and lays down the formula with which we are all familiar, of equality of status obtaining between these respective bodies. With that great objective obtained in the manner in which it was by the governments of the British commonwealth of nations, I fail to see why we may not be able in this dominion to work out a solution of our own immediate problem as between the provinces and the dominion.
All I wish to make clear this afternoon is that the task is not as easy as by some,

it may be assumed to be. To effect the desired end, it may require a step here and a step there, proceeding little by little, one step at a time, rather than attempting something that may prove after all so considerable that it will fail to get the support that it should.
I wish to add just this further word in conclusion. I believe, as my right hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) does, that this question is one which should be discussed free from party considerations. I believe he, too, holds the view that I am about to express, namely, that the question is so large that its discussion should not be confined to parliament. I believe it is a question which ought to be considered by those who are interested in constitutional problems, whether they are in this House of Commons or in the Senate or outside of parliament altogether. I would hope that as a result of my right hon. friend having brought the subject to the fore as he has to-day, and it having received preliminary consideration this afternoon, we would find that those who are interested in constitutional questions in the several provinces would take up this matter in a serious way, giving it the further thought and study that they may find it possible to give, and that they would give to the country the benefit of their views by communications to or articles in the press or by addresses before legal, political science or other bodies which it might be appropriate for them to address. I am inclined to feel that if a discussion of the kind should take place, and I believe it will, it would go a long way towards formulating public opinion on this all-important question. If there is one problem above another which can only be satisfactorily settled as a result of a united public opinion it certainly is that of the alteration of our constitution or the creation of a new constitution to supplant that under which thus far this country has been governed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
I and those who sit with me in this corner of the chamber feel that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) has performed a distinct service by bringing this matter to the attention of the house at this time. Whether we could have had a better discussion if the various groups had been notified, I do not know; possibly a spontaneous discussion of questions of this kind may be better than a set debate, where a great deal of material may be gathered that does not contribute greatly to the light shed upon the question. Members who have sat in this house for a number of years know that we in this comer have been

Constitutional Conference-Mr. Maclnnis
insistent in season and out of season in drawing to the attention of parliament the matter of dominion and provincial relations. It was, I believe, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) who moved the resolution that led up to the appointment of a committee in 1935. I believe that the discussion this afternoon has demonstrated that the people of Canada are in a better frame of mind than ever before to deal with this matter. For that reason the present government have an opportunity, such as no previous government ever had, of dealing effectively with the questions we are now discussing. They are in a much better position than the preceding government, because since 1930 tremendous changes have taken place in Canada. The preceding government and possibly the members of the present government did not realize a few years ago the import and the extent of social and economic changes which have taken place. We all realize now that we can never go back to where we were before 1930, that we are living in a new world, and that because of that fact we shall have to develop instruments of legislation and administration effectively to meet these new conditions.
What impelled me, however, to say a word now at this time was the statement made by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) with regard to the danger of communist and socialist forces displacing our democratic institutions.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: And fascists.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: I am not going to speak for either communists or fascists. Their representatives here, if they have any, can speak for them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: Who are they?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
Possibly my hon. friend knows better than I. But I think I can speak for socialists, because I am a socialist, and by reason of that I am here. Not only that, but I had an opportunity last summer of visiting various countries that have governments which are socialist to a more or less degree, and I did not see in those countries any danger to democracy. As a matter of fact, the only safeguard of democracy is socialism, because you can have democracy only when it is based upon an economy of equality, and it is because economic systems are not based upon equality that communism and fascism have developed their ideas of government by force. Communism as we know it to-day had its development in Russia, and every one with a knowledge of history knows there was no other
means by which the working class of Russia could express itself than illegally and in such underground ways as it did express itself. That is the price which every nation must pay for repression and ignorance. I suggest to hon. members that if they want to maintain democracy they can maintain it only by allowing the people an opportunity to express ideas and by making available to them those educational institutions whereby they can secure an understanding of the fundamentals of human society and human relationships.
I visited Norway. There they have had a labour socialist government for the last year or so, working not wholly by itself but in conjunction with the farmer party. I saw there no danger to democratic institutions. I visited Denmark, where the social democratic party has been the government of the country with a clear majority in the lower house for a number of years, and this year got a majority of one in the upper house. I saw there no danger to democratic institutions. I visited Sweden, where they have had a social democratic government working in cooperation with the farmer group for the past three years, and I saw no danger there to democratic institutions. If ever I saw free peoples and democracy in operation it was in those countries. We have much to learn from them.
There came to my attention yesterday a short item in a British weekly, the New Statesman and Nation, referring to the socialist government in Sweden. It says:
The socialist government in Sweden gets much less attention in this country than its achievements deserve. In the king's speech, delivered this week in the Riksdag, it was able to announce a new program which bears eloquent testimony to the success of its measures for coping with the economic crisis. Unemployment in Sweden has been so far reduced as now to present no more than a problem of seasonal variation in the demand for labour. Estimated revenue is up by more than ten per cent without any increase in taxation. The period of borrowing for public works is definitely over, and the government has been for some time past repaying debts incurred during the crisis. With the best economic advice at its command-'for Sweden is emphatically a country where economists of advanced views have played an important part in the shaping of policy-the special crisis taxes are being maintained, and the proceeds applied to the repayment of debt. At the same time, the government is actively pursuing its program of social legislation. Its new measures include legislation dealing with child welfare and mother's pensions, as well as special grants for rural housing and an improved standard of salaries for elementary school teachers and other low paid government employees.
That is a government under a social democratic party.
284	COMMONS
Constitutional Conference-Mr. Maclnnis

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: It is a unitary government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: It is a government in cooperation with the farmer group.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: I say it is unitary. There are no provinces.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: I admit that, and because of that it is easier to operate than the government in this country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. member consider the definition of a socialist in Sweden the same as the definition of a socialist in Canada?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: Decidedly. I found no difference between my point of view and that of the socialists I met in Norway, or Denmark, or Sweden, or the British Isles, or France, or any of the other countries that I visited. There is no difference. A socialist is a person who believes in the social ownership of those things necessary for the production and distribution of the means by which we live, and their democratic operation. Briefly that is a definition of socialism.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit me to ask him another question? Did he find that the trend of the social democratic party in Sweden was toward social ownership?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
I asked that question of a man who held a very prominent position in the socialist movement, and I have no hesitation in stating in this house his reply to me. I was very anxious to learn what their program of socialization for the next few years was, and he made this statement: At the present time we are not greatly concerned with the socialization of industry; as long as industry operates without undue exploitation of either workers or consumers we are not particularly concerned about who owns industry. But note this:	He stated
further: Our trade unions are , so strongly organized that they can prevent undue exploitation on the workers' side and our cooperative movement is so strong that it can take care of the consumers in the matter of exploitation; if at any time, however, we come to the point where the labour movement and the cooperative movement are not able to perform these functions we shall then deal with the question of the socialization of industry.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: That is not what the hon. member said the first time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: That is what I said. It is merely a matter of proceeding in a particular way. Possibly my hon. friend thinks that certain ideas in which you may believe you can put into effect regardless of the circumstances and the environment in which you find yourself. No intelligent person, however, proceeds upon that assumption because that cannot possibly be done if you are to work and live within the framework of democracy.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
Does the hon. gentleman
subscribe to the doctrine of socialism in Sweden, as his own doctrine of socialism?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
I have answered that
question. I do not hesitate to say that I certainly subscribe to it if I have never subscribed to anything else.
Another point was raised by the hon. member for Kootenay East with which I agree. He emphasized-and it is well that it should be emphasized-the condition in which hundreds of thousands of people, as he said, in the various provinces find themselves at the present time. On going among these people this is what I find. They say: That cannot be done or this cannot be done under any provincial government because we have not the power. The people have lost hope entirely in parliament doing anything for them, and that hope can be restored only by parliament proving to them that something can and will be done.
I am in favour of maintaining the basis of confederation. I cannot see that a province can improve its, position in any way by leaving confederation, because for every restriction or evil it might get away from it would meet half a dozen others. For that reason I believe it is folly for any province, whether it be in the east or in the west, to talk of secession.
I do not wish to take up any more time, because the present discussion anticipates one that will take place within a few days in connection with a resolution which is on the order paper. I shall content myself with these remarks, simply pointing out to the Prime Minister tMr. Mackenzie King) that he and his government have an opportunity to do things that never before could have been done in Canada.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
In
rising to speak to the suggestion that has been made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), I do so merely to emphasize from my point of view the importance of it. As I listened to the Prime Minister

Constitutional Conference-Mr. Walsh
(Mr. Mackenzie King), one phrase in his remarks caught my attention; he said that he would find a way or make one. It gives me great encouragement to hear words of that sort, coming as they do from the Prime Minister, and I hope that statement presages a new policy under his leadership.
We have heard this afternoon a great deal in connection with the method of procedure. To me, as a layman, this matters very little so long as we accomplish the object we have in view. To-day we are not confronted with a problem any greater or more difficult to solve than that which faced the fathers of confederation during the years from 1860 to 1867. They found a way or they made one, and we in our day and generation can do something similar and bestow a like blessing on the generations that are to follow us in this dominion.
I do not wish to obtrude anything of a political nature into a debate of this kind, but I should like to make one reference to a suggestion which was made so frequently during the course of the election of October, 1935. I think it should be repeated in this house and in connection with the subject matter which is now before us for discussion. The Prime Minister and those associated with him will remember that they emphasized, not at one meeting, but continuously at all the meetings, the fact that most, if not all, of the provincial governments were of the Liberal persuasion and that it would be well for the electors of Canada to return a government of a similar complexion to hold the reins of office at Ottawa. That was emphasized, and, if we may judge by the results, to good effect. The Prime Minister always followed that statement with this suggestion, that the Conservative party could not possibly cooperate with those occupying the seats of government in the various provinces, their political complexion being what it was, whereas his party would be in a position to cooperate; that his first effort on becoming Prime Minister of Canada would be to call immediately a conference of those provinces, the governments of which were for the most part of the same political persuasion as his own party, and that out of that conference there would come a remedy for the evils and the distress brought about-so the present Prime Minister said on that occasion-by the government which had been in office during the five previous years.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
He hoped it
would come.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
He hoped he would find a way out? Well, I would remind him that his
government have been in power now for a year and a half. They have had the opportunity of many conferences with provincial representatives; yet we do not see emerging any solution of the problems with which we were confronted in 1935 and as we are confronted with in 1937. I also suggest that conditions existing in this country are not going to right themselves with a laissez faire attitude on our part. It is useless for the present government to sit back and hope that good times are going to provide a remedy for conditions which now prevail. Less than two weeks ago it was my privilege to listen to the chairman of the National Employment Commission, and on that occasion he gave utterance to a statement which has been made many times from this side of the house, that conditions which at present prevail in connection with unemployment will not be cured by good times, no matter how good they may be, in the immediate future. He felt that unemployment was a condition which would remain with us after we passed through the period of good times that now seems to be coming. We must find a solution for that problem. I have no doubt that most hon. members have had many communications from those who are in distress. I receive them especially from the younger element in this country, and in particular from my own province. If we can sit idly by and allow a pointed suggestion of this kind to be passed over lightly, in view of the conditions under which these young people are living it is time we had some radical change in our method of government and of procedure.
I emphasize this point in view of the discussion on the possibility of amendment of the British North America Act in order to make it more effective. That act was passed as a result of many conferences. It did not have its roots altogether in those conferences which immediately preceded the passing of the act. It had its roots away back in Canadian history, as far back as 1763. It had its roots in the Quebec Act of 1774, in the Constitutional Act of 1791, in the Act of Union of 1841. In all those acts, and in the British North America Act, certain guarantees were given to minorities in certain provinces of the dominion. I always voice the warning that if we contemplate any change in the British North America Act the proposal must be accompanied by the assertion that in no way will the fundamental principles underlying that act be changed.
We have in Canada nine provincial governments and a federal government. Last evening it was my privilege to speak before a gathering
286	COMMONS
Constitutional Conference-Mr. Walsh
of retail business men, men doing business in a small way in this country, men who have known days of adversity in the past and are just emerging from such phase now and looking forward hopefully to the future. Those men are considering the problems of the day, and one of the problems which I discussed with them was that of taxation. We reached the conclusion that there was not so much to be said against taxation as such but there was something very definite to be said about the overlapping which prevails in the field of taxation. We also spoke of overlapping in other fields, in jurisdiction and in the work of various departments of government. I want to emphasize what came out of that meeting. We are overtaxed in this country, but I believe that overtaxation can be remedied by the suggestion that we have before us to-day. The problem is not so much the burden of taxation as such; it is the burden of overlapping taxation. This is due to lack of understanding of the proper division of jurisdiction in connection with governmental work. Let me take one example: We have a federal sales tax. In the city of Montreal we have a municipal sales tax. Should there be a provincial sales tax, a municipal sales tax, as well as the federal tax, or should not some adjustment be made between the federal and municipal and provincial governments in order that the federal government shall have jurisdiction in connection with sales tax and the provincial and municipal governments shall have control over other forms of taxation? Is it not time that a genuine conference was called, in a real effort to alleviate distress in this country? And one way of alleviating that distress is by removing part of the burden of taxation. I cannot understand why men of good common sense can not agree on certain principles, particularly in the field of taxation. We know the provinces have to have revenue; we know the municipalities have to have revenue, and of course the federal government has to have revenue. Revenue can be derived from certain fields. Could those fields not be satisfactorily apportioned between the province and the dominion so that their jurisdictions will be clearly defined, and overlapping entirely done away with? If that were done the people would have a much smaller burden to bear. That is one point I desire to emphasize particularly.
In closing, let me say I was happy to listen to the remarks of the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens), and I was extremely happy when I heard the Prime Minister make such a bold statement, that

he was going to find a way or make one. May there be more of such assertions and more power to carry them into effect.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance): I desire to detain the house only a very few minutes. I have perhaps attended as many conferences between the dominion and the provinces as any other hon. member. I believe I have attended, on one side or the other, all that have taken place since about 1916, except those which occurred during the last five years, and I appreciate very much the tone of the discussion to-day, because it seems to me that it goes back in spirit to that which alone made confederation possible in the first place, such a concentrated desire on the part of the Canadian people to achieve unity that they were willing to drop political differences much more acute and much more violent in their manifestation than any which prevail to-day. We speak of procedure, but we must not ignore the importance of evoking again that spirit. I believe the question of procedure would be materially reduced in its importance if only the Canadian people could become as seized of the vital importance of adjusting these difficulties in our national life and our national constitution as were their forebears during the two or three decades which preceded 1867. I know it is difficult to expect the same degree of public interest which prevailed then. In spite of the lack of easy communication; in spite of the comparative lack of freely circulating mediums in any way comparable with those which are in existence to-day, I believe that public interest occupied a larger place in the life of the individual Canadian during the two decades prior to confederation than it does to-day. In those days public affairs were a more general topic of discussion in the home. These matters we have been discussing this afternoon were generally understood by a much larger proportion of the population than is the case with the much better educated population we have to-day. There were not the diversions; there were no movies; there was no radio; there were very few theatres. Men and women tended more to have their minds occupied with really vital matters than is the case to-day. An hon. member opposite shakes his head. I agree with him that very probably there is a larger aggregate number of students of these questions to-day. I am speaking more particularly of the degree of interest on the part of the whole population.

Constitutional Conference-Mr. Dunning
However, Mr. Speaker, what I rose to say was this, that to the extent that the addresses to which we have listened this afternoon can contribute toward a non-partisan discussion of this matter, to that extent they will tend to increase the possibility of success in any conference which may take place, call it what you will. What happens at every dominion-provincial conference? As I say, I have been at many of them. Every government, be it Liberal, or Tory, or United Farmers of Alberta, or anything else, provincial or dominion, which attends such a conference, is conscious all the time it is there that it has an opposition back home.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
That must be so; it
cannot be avoided. Also, if it is a provincial government, it knows perfectly well that if, as a provincial government, it makes at that conference any concession whatever or does anything which can be interpreted as a concession, the opposition party back home, no matter whether it be Liberal, or Tory, or Labour, or United Farmers of Alberta, or Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, will immediately raise the cry of provincial rights as against that particular provincial government.
These are the cold, hard facts with respect to every dominion-provincial conference which takes place, and I submit that these cold, hard facts are likely to continue to exist unless we can find an approach to the problem comparable with the approach which was created prior to and including the year 1867. Methods have been suggested to-day whereby that approach might be developed along lines which would prevent such considerations as oppositions back home being vital in their ability to prevent success being attained. I have no particular views as to whether such a gathering should be a constituent assembly or a constitutional conference. I should be very content to allow those who know the meaning of terms better than I do to determine the kind of gathering it should be. What I rose to speak of was the spirit which must animate this nation before any such gathering can possibly attain the objective we all have in mind.
During the past year, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has indicated, we had a dominion-provincial conference along the lines suggested by the House of Commons committee of 1935. I believe every man attending that conference really laboured conscientiously to the end that something
of value to Canada might result. All were subject to the limitations to which I have been referring. Some good did result, but the great core of the problem was not grappled with effectively. It was talked about, as we have talked about it for the last twenty or twenty-five years to my knowledge. It was not really grappled with.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
One of the difficulties,
as the minister realizes, was that if the conference of last year were to succeed those attending it would have to take views exactly opposite to those they had taken for the previous five years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not quite understand that, because the conference was composed of representatives of all governments, and I do not carry in my mind the degree to which changes in the political complexions of the provinces may have taken place within the last five years. But, however that may be, from the point of view from which I am attempting to deal with the question it would not make a bit of difference if the governments represented there were Liberal, or Conservative, or Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, or Social Credit or anything else. In the very nature of things they would have to take into account the people back home, and more particularly the opposition back home. I know that no man in practical politics would dispute that suggestion.
Out of the meeting held last year arose the suggestion that for the first time in Canada's history we might at least attempt to set up a cooperative body which, without having any powers whatever, would study means of cooperating with respect to financial and taxation problems as between the dominion and the provinces. I am quite sure that the student of history will regard it as strange that in all the time since confederation, with the divided responsibilities, the divided powers and the divided fields of taxation which exist in Canada, until now no effort has been made to form a cooperative bod3T which would continuously study these matters and continuously endeavour to find a basis of cooperation among the different provinces themselves and between the provinces and the Dominion of Canada. An effort was made, as I say, to set up such a body.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
It is the negation of
responsible government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
Surely there could be a discussion and an examination by such a body of men without in any way creating, as my right hon. friend suggests, a negation
288	COMMONS
Constitutional Conference-Mr. Dunning
of responsible government. Surely it is possible for a body of ministers representing different sovereignties to gather together from year to year in order to see how they can effectively cooperate in a common sense way in connection with common problems; yet that has not been systematically done in the whole history of our confederation.
This is a day for frankness, and I shall be frank. Sometimes I wonder if I have not made more trouble for myself and for the government of Canada than the idea is worth in having sponsored the national finance council or committee idea. When the committee met it was quite obvious that a number of members regarded it as another dominion-provincial conference-which it was not at all-at which they were privileged to stand up, one after another, and simply ask the dominion for something. There was only one approach to problem after problem: "Will the dominion give the provinces this, that or the other in a financial way?" or, "Will the dominion yield up to the provinces this, that or the other source of revenue which it now enjoys?" I do not wish it to be understood that I am blaming the provinces. Goodness knows they are finding it difficult enough to carry on their work. I mention these facts merely to illustrate the difficulties of the problem we are discussing. Without breaking the agreed-upon confidence concerning details of discussion, I might state that as chairman I said on the last day to the assembly, "Well, gentlemen, we have accomplished something-not, I am sure, as much as any of us desired-in the interests of the people we represent. I am wondering, after listening to the discussions and to the development of this and that impossibility, if it is worth while to have a national finance committee for the voluntary discussion of these matters." Man after man got up and said, "No question about it; we must continue; we must continue to try." That gave me some encouragement, especially after three or four days of disagreement not merely between the provinces and the dominion, but disagreements emphasizing the widest possible diversity of views in many matters between province and province.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
To me it was an encouragement. After that experience, difficult as it was, every provincial representative said, "By all means, we must continue to try." That, I believe, is the approach which we must all have to this problem. I do hope we are successful in recreating the spirit out oi which this nation was born-a greater 
interest on the part of the mass of the people, not in their own particular grievances as such, but in the supreme desirability of once more accomplishing unity in confederation, and through that unity attaining the power to deal with grievances which are all too real.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) has brought to the attention of parliament and of Canada what I believe is at this time a very serious problem in this country, but as was pointed out by the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) this afternoon, there are on the order paper various resolutions under which this subject may be discussed at considerable length and perhaps with better preparation by all concerned. However, now that we are on the subject, it might be well to inquire why an attempt was made to bring it to the attention of the house to-day.
So far as the feeling of the people of Canada is concerned, I have no doubt that they desire-and they have so expressed themselves at various times-to bring about certain amendments to the British North America Act, but the leader of the opposition has, I believe, misconstrued their reasons for wanting this done. As was pointed out this afternoon by the Minister of Justice, provincial jurisdiction has never been questioned by the people of the various provinces; nearly always the question has been one of obtaining greater powers for the provincial governments.
Just a few days ago we heard in this house a good deal about the British Empire and its component parts, and also a great deal about the autonomy of its various units, each independent, but all allied under the one crown. It was pointed out with pride that these governments exercised great powers; that they were jealous of those powers, but that nevertheless harmony existed between them. A similar contention might be advanced so far as Canada and its provinces are concerned, for, after all, any changes sought in the British North America Act are the result of the agitation of the people in the various provinces. When we hear of such a proposal as that made to-day, and especially when the reason given in support of it is that it is for the preservation of certain institutions in view of the things that are happening in

Constitutional Conference-Mr. Pelletier
various provinces to-day, one wonders what institutions are demanding that such a conference should be held in this country at this time. That is a salient point, it appears to me, and I shall leave it at that because it is my intention to go into the matter more deeply when various other resolutions on the order paper come before the house.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, little or no headway will be made by any agreement between the provinces and the dominion until some definite attitude is taken on the principle whether more power should be granted to the provinces or whether their powers should be curtailed. Until we have adopted some principle on the question of either granting more power or curtailing the present powers of the provinces, it seems to me that it would be impossible, as was pointed out this afternoon by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), for any such conference to come to an agreement. Before sitting down I would again ask why, in view of the resolutions on the order paper touching on this very subject, this matter should have been brought up in the house to-day.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the gravity of the subject matter under discussion impels me to express my views in respect thereto. It is regrettable that on a subject matter such as this we should have had a political partisan address such as was made by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot). The hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), in speaking to the question, pointed out that if we were to maintain this democracy, it must demonstrate its efficiency as compared with an autocracy or a dictatorship. I must confess, after listening to the speech made by the hon. member for Temiscouata, that I was somewhat doubtful of the efficiency of that part of a democracy which selected him to represent them in the House of Commons, but my faith was restored when I listened to the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning).
The Minister of Justice did not tell us specifically what his views were with respect to the proposal of the hon. leader of the opposition, and if he was speaking on behalf of the government he gave us no specific statement as to their attitude or policy with respect to the matter. But as I listened to his delicacy of word and his eloquence of diction in a language which was not his mother tongue, my faith in the efficiency of democracy was greatly restored.
The Minister of Finance made the statement that this discussion would, if nothing else, engender among the people of this country a unanimity of opinion which was essential to the enactment of amendments to the British North America Act. I wonder if the Minister of Finance has failed to appreciate that there is in Canada a tremendous consensus of opinion with respect to this subject matter. In the riding I represent I polled in the last election, something over
11,000	votes; the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation candidate polled something over 8,000; the Liberal candidate, something over
7,000,	and the Reconstruction candidate, something over 4,000. But I venture to suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if you took a poll of all these voters who voted in the last election, irrespective of what party they may have supported, 90 per cent of them would support the amending of the British North America Act.
The hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) said that there was a growing feeling of futility and hopelessness among the Canadian people with respect to their parliaments. I must confess that as a member of one of their parliaments I have had a growing feeling of futility and hopelessness with respect to securing those amendments to the British North America Act which are essential if we are going to carry out in this country those social measures, sometimes called by my friends to my left, measures of social justice, which are essential to maintain this democracy. Surely dominion and provincial conferences have proven conclusively, for the reasons so well stated by the Minister of Finance, if for no other, that you cannot through that channel get that unanimity of opinion which may be required. Even in respect of the matter of uniformity of laws in the provinces how many conferences have been held, how little headway has been made I It is all very well to say that they agreed upon a uniform companies act, may I ask which of the provinces have put into effect an act that is in terms of the act of the Dominion of Canada? If we have such difficulty in obtaining uniform laws in respect of one or two branches of our civil law in the provinces, how little chance we have of getting that unanimity of opinion and view which is required if we are going to obtain amendments to the British North America Act through the channel of provincial and dominion conferences.
I should have been very happy had the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) either intimated an acceptance of the scheme proposed by my honoured leader or suggested

lQ	COMMONS
Constitutional Conference-Mr. Lawson____
some specific steps which the government contemplated taking toward obtaining the very-necessary amendments. It is all very well to say that a committee of this house made a report in 1935, but may I ask what action has been taken in respect of that report? None. I beg pardon; I should not have said "none." Let me put it in this way no effective action has been taken. The Prime Minister intimated this afternoon that a dominion-provincial conference was called.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: That was the sole recommendation.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
I quite agree, and the
Prime Minister quite frankly stated to the house that he could not say that as a result of that conference any real advancement toward the ultimate goal had been obtained. Now, sir, the Prime Minister emphasized by the statement and the reiteration of it that all parties in this house, and, I infer, all parties in the legislatures of the different provinces, were favourable to an amendment, but that it was the manner of procedure which created the difficulty and the obstacle. Then, if I understood the Prime Minister correctly, he finished by saying that the government had contemplated the appointment of a commission or committee to study the whole problem, but felt that to do so^ while the cases with respect to the jurisdiction of the dominion or the provinces were before the privy council would be taking precipitate action. May I point out that there is no problem before the judicial committee of the privy council with respect to the method of procedure of amending the British North America Act. What, is before the judicial committee of the privy council is the question whether this parliament had power to enact certain measures commonly called social or paternal legislation, such as unemployment insurance, maximum hours of labour, minimum rates of wages, and so forth. Surely, if our problem to-day of securing the amendment of the British North America Act is one of procedure only, the pending cases before the judicial committee of the privy council can in no measure constitute an obstacle in our path. No one realizes better than I the difficulties in the road of amending our constitution. No one will lend more sympathetic support than I to any really effective measure which may be taken by the government to bring about the very much desired end. But at the moment we have before this house a specific proposal from the hon. leader of the opposition, a specific proposal which, in my

opinion, is worthy not merely of consideration but of support. Surely, I suggest, with that specific proposal before this parliament, it is incumbent upon the present government, if they desire to obtain the amendments necessary to vest in this parliament nation-wide powers to deal with these social measures of legislation, to accept that specific proposal or, in the alternative, to propose some other specific measures which should be taken.
In conclusion-

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
With that applause from the hon. member for Temiscouata I might be tempted to continue. I wish to impress particularly upon the Minister of Finance, in view of the expressions which he gave so eloquently to this house immediately preceding the six o'clock recess, that there is in Canada a tremendous body of public opinion in favour of amending the British North America Act, especially for the purpose of enabling the enactment of national measures dealing with social legislation and national schemes for the reduction of taxation and the eradication of the duplication of governmental services between the provinces and the dominion. If there is that preponderance of opinion which I believe there is, then I ask, How can you bring about the expression of that opinion when the Prime Minister says the matter is merely one of procedure? I can hardly agree with that statement in its entirety. In my opinion what it lacks is this:	The public who have a crystallized
opinion in favour of this amendment do not know where to express their opinion by pressure. When they go to a member of the legislature he says: Oh, it is something that has to be done by the dominion parliament. When they go to their member who represents them in the House of Commons, he says: Oh, it is something we cannot do without the consent of the provinces. I suggest, sir, that a constitutional conference such as that proposed by my leader would give an opportunity for that crystallized public opinion which exists in this country to make itself felt upon the representatives to that conference, be they representatives of legislatures or of this parliament, in so unmistakable a way that there would soon be brought about the desired amendment to the British North America Act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee of supply, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

Supply-Public Works

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE

speakeroldname: Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Public Works):
maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: Before the different items included in these estimates are called, I desire to state, just in a word, that these estimates are what may be described as necessary for carrying on the business of the different departments. They provide for the maintenance upkeep, repairs; heating and lighting of all the public buildings which the dominion government controls. No question of policy is involved in any of these items; they are those which are necessary for properly carrying on the business of the federal government. They are items that have come before the house regularly for a number of years and with very few exceptions they are all the same. The items that are not for maintenance of service or for taking care of public buildings are for necessary works or for the completion of contracts or works already started. The first vote is for a public building at Berwick, Nova Scotia. It is a revote.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
I wish to thank the
minister for his opening explanation, which may facilitate the passage of some of these items. However, I would ask him for a further statement as to the policy of the government as suggested by these estimates. The estimates of last year included a number of items for which provision had been made in the Public Works Construction Acts of 1934 and 1935, items which had been in detail passed upon and approved by this parliament, and for which the necessary moneys had been appropriated following those acts. For a reason which was explained at the time these items which had already been provided for were gathered up and included in the estimates of last year.
. ^ hjit I wish to point out to the minister is this: ^ In the summary of appropriations for public works we find that in 1936 and 1937 the amount appropriated in the manner I have mentioned is $15,570,000 odd, and included in that there was a small sum of $544,000 authorized by statute. For the coming year, 1937-38, the total amount included in these estimates to be voted is $11,277,000 odd, showing a decrease of $3,754,000. I recall very well that in opposition the members of the present government strongly urged that the government should embark upon an extensive program of public works for ^ the relief of unemployment, and I am anxious to know whether the fact that the estimates of this year amount to the figure I have mentioned, or about $3,750,000 less than the estimates of last year, indicates a reversal of policy in that direction. Have
the government decided that it is advisable to reduce by this amount the appropriations for public works? Have they abandoned the contention that increased expenditures in this direction will stimulate employment, will help the construction industry and will be of general advantage? These are questions to which I think the committee would like to have some answers from the minister. Following that, possibly I may have one or two other questions to ask. In this connection, however, I would note that the estimates, as far as I have been able to observe, do not contain any items of expenditure under the head of capital; and generally we have had some items of capital expenditure in connection with .public works. Does that mean that the government have abandoned any program similar to that carried on by former governments in this respect? Do they contemplate the construction in Ottawa of any public buildings which under ordinary circumstances would be charged to capital account? These are items which occur to me at the moment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
There is no change in policy on the part of the party now in power. We have always been of opinion that it was much better to spend money on public works or public undertakings than to give it away in the form of relief, and we are in favour of that policy to-day just as we were when in opposition. The reason why numerous items for new constructions are not included in these estimates is that the government felt that in the main estimates we should disclose to the committee what is absolutely necessary for taking care of public buildings, looking after repairs, maintenance, lighting, heating and so on, and that we should not burden the main estimates with a new list of projects and undertakings, which though they might be necessary from a certain point of view, are not essential to the propeT administration of public affairs. It was with that idea in mind that we began last year by reducing to a large extent the amounts included in the main estimates apart from the necessary money to complete works already undertaken. This year we are again reducing to the very minimum the items that might be proposed to the committee for new undertakings. That is why the main estimates have been reduced to the extent indicated by my hon. friend. I am sure that he has in mind-it will probably be the next question he will ask-the question whether there are going to be any supplementary estimates. I hope there will; I hope to be dn a position to convince the Minister of Finance that we should have supplementary estimates.

Supply-Public Works
As regards buildings in Ottawa, generally enumerated under the head of capital expenditures, consideration was given last year to the proposal to build a supreme court house. Plans were prepared and a study was made of the site upon which such a building might be erected. I regret, however, to say that after the preliminary designs and the plans prepared in the department were gone over we were afraid that the site we had in mind would be too small to permit the erection of the heavy buildings contemplated last year and designed by the architects of the department. But the government still have in mind and are determined to build in Ottawa certainly one additional building, for housing the Supreme Court of Canada at least, and possibly the exchequer court. This question will be considered by the government when an opportunity is presented to discuss the possibility of supplementary estimates with the Minister of Finance.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
I thank the minister for his comprehensive explanation. I rather expected him to express the hope that there would be supplementary estimates. In my fairly long experience in this house I have never known a Minister of Public Works who did not have that hope. Possibly the hopes of some hon. members on his side of the chamber will be encouraged. I am sure, however, that their hopes will not all be fulfilled, unless conditions greatly differ from those the minister has outlined.
As to the capital expenditure at Ottawa, I rather expected that the item' would appear in these estimates, notwithstanding that there may be a difference of opinion as to the site. Often the site of a public building is determined after provision is voted for the construction of the building. I notice that in the rotunda at the entrance to the Commons chamber is placed a very interesting model of the suggested arrangement of some of these buildings. I assume the site to which the minister refers as being controversial is shown somewhere on that model. I know that in the past the same question has caused a good deal of difficulty. The minister has_ my sympathy in his efforts to reconcile conflicting opinions as to the location of this building. That controversy has existed for years and is one of the factors which has delayed the construction.
Can the minister tell the committee at this stage the amounts which have been expended, say, prior to the end of 1936, under the provisions of the Public Works Construction Act of 1934 and the Supplementary Public Works Construction Act of 1935? Also could he

without too much trouble, either now or at a subsequent sitting of the committee, give a list of the projects or items provided for thereby which have not yet been undertaken?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
According to the statement I have before me the expenditure under the Public Works Construction Acts was, for the fiscal year 1934-35, $5,916,559, and for the fiscal year 1935-36, $17,878,406.52.
As to the list of projects contemplated but not yet carried out,. I thank my hon. friend for giving me an opportunity of saying that I am not at the moment in a position to give him a statement, but I assure him that the projects which have been abandoned are not very numerous. Practically all of them have been carried on. I will, however, undertake to give the list.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: I assume that a number of those projects are still not completed, but to be completed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: They are practically all completed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister spoke of the policy of the government and its adherence to the belief that public moneys might well be expended for public works rather than in direct relief. Of course there is nothing new about that. During the term of office of the previous government public moneys were expended, in cooperation with the provinces, for public works having for their object the relief of unemployment. I notice that the present government are still continuing that policy, under the agreements made with the different provinces; that is, they are undertaking, in cooperation with the provinces, works for the relief of unemployment. But that leaves out of the program the direct expenditure of moneys on account of the dominion government for the relief of unemployment by the construction of buildings and the undertaking of public works. I do not want to press the matter too far at this stage, because I know the minister's estimates have been brought down fairly early, and the session is in its early stages. I hope the supplementary estimates will disclose something which in a measure will remedy this apparent oversight.
New Brunswick
Moncton-old post office building-improvements and repairs, $11,100.
Saint John quarantine station-Partridge island-improvements, alterations and repairs, $7,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
I notice there are some improvements to be made to the old post office building at Moncton. I may say that

Supply-Public Works-Buildings
they have a very fine new post office there, of which the citizens are proud. What use is to be made of the old post office building in that city?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: The repairs to the old building are being made for the accommodation of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: I should also like an explanation with reference to "appropriations not required for 1937-38." I note that there was $44,000 unexpended last year. I assume that is for public works started but not completed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: No. I admit I was not very clear myself as to the meaning of those words, which are found all through the estimates. This is not my responsibility. These words are added by the Department of Finance to all the estimates for a purpose which I confess I do not understand very well. In reality they mean this: They include in what is indicated in the estimates as appropriations not required for 1937-38 all the money voted for projects which have been completed. That is why I cannot understand it. All the projects undertaken under an item of the estimates, and completed during the year are put together; officials of the Department of Finance add the amounts up and at the end of our estimates say, "Appropriations not required for 1937-38." Probably the idea is that it is not going to be necessary to revote that money or to rebuild the building which has been completed. In all fairness, however, I am quite ready to admit that there may be good reason for this item from the point of view of accounting in the Department of Finance, but I confess my complete ignorance as to the reason for it. After having had that question put to me last year by both new and old members I tried to have some light thrown upon the matter, and this is the only explanation I have been able to secure. When I look up the list of projects completed during the past year, the total voted for those buildings which have been completed, as far as I can see, is the appropriation not required. That is the only explanation I can give. It may not be very convincing or very clear, but I believe it is a fact. As I have said, there may be very good reason for doing it in this way from the point of view of the Department of Finance, but I have no other explanation to offer than the one I have given.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: I wish to thank the minister for his very clear explanation. As I understand it, in New Brunswick we have $18,000 voted for buildings that are not completed and $44,000 for buildings that have been completed?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: No; the $44,000 was voted in last year's estimates, and that money is not to be voted again this year. That has been spent on the projects which have been completed. The amount provided this year is $18,100, but that amount covers only two items, the Moncton post office building and the Saint John quarantine station. There may, of course, be something in the supplementary estimates.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
I really cannot help congratulating the minister upon his explanation of this item. It is different from the explanation I have always given, but I am not sure that it is not just as good or perhaps a little better. Somehow or another I thought that the money voted but not required to complete buildings, or something of that sort, was covered up in these items. However, there are many explanations, and after all it is a bookkeeping matter.
I see the amount voted for the Saint John quarantine station is $7,000, which was the amount voted last year. Under this expenditure does the minister contemplate any extension of or addition to the buildings, and would he care to say what is to be the policy of the government in connection with immigration, whether it will require any extension of the existing building, or whether this just covers repairs and maintenance?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: The amount of $7,000 is required for small repairs to be undertaken to the buildings already in existence. We do not contemplate any extension of the present buildings, or any new construction. I can give the amounts estimated, if that is required.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: Not if it is only for ordinary repairs; I would not ask that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE

speechtext:

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister if representations were made asking for some improvements to the public building at Summerside, Prince Edward Island.  moved to the ground floor. If that were done, the upper part of the building could be used by the mounted police, or for some other purpose. speechtext: Of course my hon. friend will understand that under this vote we cannot provide for the construction of any buildings. So far as the other question is concerned, at the moment I cannot say whether any representations have been received asking for the enlargement of the existing building, but knowing the activity of my hon. friend and how alive he is to all that concerns Prince Edward Island, I am quite sure that if the need has been suggested to him he has made representations, and I should not be surprised to find his letter in the records of the department.

may I s:.y that there is no hon. member for whom I have greater respect than for the Minister o<f Public Works. A new policy seems to have been embarked upon, which in my judgment and in that of my constituents-and after all they count-

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE

for twenty-three years. In the immigration office at Halifax, where in former years a local caterer was employed we now have one sent from this part of the country. Local positions should be filled by local people. If everything is to be drawn from the centre and the extremities are to be forgotten, we might as well make up our minds that we are going to lose our feet; then we shall not be able to walk and shall have to go back to the cradle.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: There is no discrimination at all in favour of Quebec. speechtext: Without wishing to criticize, may I say I am informed that the number of public buildings in Prince Edward Island is almost as great as the number in Quebec.

speechtext: The minister has said that the buildings are to be erected to give postal services to the communities affected. Have such buildings been requested by the Post Office Department.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: Evidently there has been no request from the Post Office Department for the erection of these two buildings.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: But not for the other one. A principle is involved in this. I do not think the Department of Public Works should put up buildings for any other department unless the department concerned applies for it. Only one building under this item has been asked for by the Post Office Department, and while the amount is comparatively small, nevertheless this country seems to be dotted all over with buildings which evidently the Post Office Department is not very anxious to operate. I have in mind one building running into considerably more money than the amount involved here, which was put up by the Public Works Department for the Post Office Department, and when the building was completed the Post Office Department refused to operate it; they said they did not require the building. If we are going to operate a public utility like the post office, the buildings comprised within that utility should, I think, be entirely wtihin the jurisdiction of the Post Office Department itself. As a matter of principle, the Department of Public Works should not construct buildings for the Post Office Department unless that department has requested them. It is all right for the minister to inform the committee that away back in 1924 some hon. member requested the department to erect a public building there, and it may be all right for the minister to tell us that the citizens of a certain locality have requested his department to erect a building, but if the minister were to put up buildings simply on the request of citizens of different parts of this dominion I am afraid there would be a public building on every street corner. The time has come for this committee and parliament to deal with these matters in a logical way. I do not think the Department of Public Works is the right and proper department to erect public buildings for another department, particularly when that other department has not requested it to do so. speechtext: I have not before me the information my hon. friend asks for. It covers only repairs to the existing buildings. I thought I had some information as to the number of patients who have been treated there, but I regret to say that it has not been given to us by the Department of National Health.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
The reason I asked the question is that I understand there were no detentions at that station during this past season. I am also informed that Grosse Isle station is of very little real use at the present time owing to improved conditions of service at the city of Quebec and generally improved conditions in travel. I understand that the immigration branch has actually withdrawn the services of the Anglican priest who was regularly stationed at Grosse Isle during the navigation season, and other curtailments have been made in order to reduce expense. Yet each year we have an item going through for repairs and renovations in connection with that station. It seems to me that probably a good number of those buildings, not being in use, could be temporarily closed without doing any real harm to Grosse Isle as a possible station for detention of any cases that might arrive in the Saint Lawrence. Would the minister entertain the possibility of consulting with the immigration branch and the department of health and seeing if it might not be possible to work along those lines and save a little of the money that we usually spend there annually, not only on buildings but on the wharf and other projects in connection with that island? I am not for a moment advocating that the island be closed as a station, because I know it might be necessary some day when we run into trouble. At the same time a number of these buildings are kept open and a considerable number of people are maintained on the island from
public funds. I understand that the population of the island, all in the service of the government, amounts roughly to a hundred people.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: I feel quite sure that the observations of the hon. member will be brought to the attention of the department of health.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: Referring again to the item of the public building for Ste. Anne de Beaupre, may I suggest to the minister that the present government are not consistent in their policy. I would refer the minister to the circumstances of the erection of the public building in the town of Burlington, Ontario. The late government appropriated $25,000 for a public building, a post office, in Burlington, but when the present government came into office they said it was too great an amount for that town, and it has been reduced to $15,000. I am quite sure that the postal revenue of the town of Burlington greatly exceeds that of Ste. Anne de Beaupre, and for that reason I protest the amount for Ste. Anne.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
I confess that at the
moment I am not in a position ito make a fair comparison between the proposed public building for Ste. Anne de Beaupre and the one proposed for the town which my hon. friend has just mentioned. But I may say this is a point on which his party is in agreement with me and I am in agreement with them. The proposal for the erection of a public building at Ste. Anne de Beaupre originated with my hon. friends when they were on this side of the house, and I am quite willing to carry on their proposal. It is a very practical one. I assume they were justified in placing in the estimates the necessary amount for that public building at Ste. Anne de Beaupre. As far as Burlington is concerned I have not the facts before me; but would my hon. friend not give me the pleasure of getting credit for economizing to some extent for the public treasury by reducing the amount of the expenditure at Burlington?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
No; I do not think
that towns in Ontario should be penalized.

included an item for that post office which I have been after for Montreal West. It also made me very happy to hear him speak of supplementary estimates. In connection with the public building at Ste. Martine, I believe Ste. Martine is a small parish in the county of Chateauguay. Is that right?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
This small town of Ste.
Martine, on the main highway from Montreal to Malone, seems to be in a rather flourishing condition as far as public buildings are concerned. It is getting more than its share. The provincial government erected a small agricultural college on the outskirts of the town, and now we see it coming into prominence with a public building at the expense of the dominion treasury. Personally f do not think Ste. Martine deserves such preferred treatment. It is a very small municipality and can be served to good advantage with a rural mail delivery rather than a regular post office. I do not think as much revenue will be derived from Ste. Martine as from the town of Bedford. I do not care to criticize the erection of public buildings in Quebec. I am very much in favour of the erection of public buildings, particularly near home and more particularly if they happen to be in my own constituency, and are needed; but this is one case where I am convinced that t'he building is not a necessity. I do not know whether it has been particularly requested or whether the previous government entertained the suggestion that it should be erected there. I only know Ste. Martine. There are no streets properly so called; there is just one long main road going through the place. The item hardly seems justified under the circumstances, particularly when I cannot get a post office erected at Montreal West, a place of
5,000	people, where the revenue would more than meet the expense of constructing a post office, and the building has been requested by the council. Possibly Ste. Martine had particular influence with the previous government; if so, it 'has continued that influence with the present government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext:
This is another case in which the two parties were in agreement. The proposal started with the Liberal administration and was approved by the following Conservative government, and as a third party I am continuing the policy pursued by my two predecessors. As regards the importance of the locality and the justification for a public building there, I hope the committee will allow me to express a private sentiment that

has been very near to my heart for quite a number of years. From the standpoint of advantage to Canada as a whole we hear a good deal about the back-to-the-land policy and the advisability of inducing those who live in our cities to go back to the rural sections. It is only fair that we should give some little encouragement, in the way of small expenditures, to the people in these outlying districts so as to make life more interesting and agreeable to them. We are spending a good deal of money that does not help those living in the rural sections-farmers, small merchants, blacksmiths and those who are trying to make a living in the small localities throughout the country-and it is only reasonable for us to show these people some consideration and to help them as far as we can to live a happy and contented life. We ought to be a little generous to them even if it costs a little more than we might be justified in spending from a purely business point of view.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: I sympathize with the minister's remarks; I am in complete agreement with him. We are all in a generous frame of mind particularly during these trying times, and we are inclined to be generous; but I suggest that our generosity must be commensurate with our ability to pay. I suggest to the minister that if the previous government commenced this post office at Ste. Martine, the people of the county of Chateauguay did not approve because they defeated the Conservative member and returned a Liberal candidate, no doubt in protest against the spending of that money in such a small place.

Peace River is a new country with great possibilities of development, and I compliment this government for giving those pioneers some assistance in the development of their country. Ontario as we know has been treated well in the past, and is no doubt well represented in this House of Commons, but the outlying districts, including Peace River, also require help, and I am very much in favour of the suggestion made by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. MacKinnon) that these pioneers should receive some assistance in developing a section which in the future will be one of Canada's most productive areas.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE
speechtext: Might I ask the minister when the item for Peace River first appeared in the public works estimates?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OP MR. BENNETT ON MOTION OP MINISTER OP FINANCE

I am glad the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence) asked that question because, representing Prince Rupert, it gives me a chance to say a few words.
